questions.q: The first bill splitter passed its only test (₦25,000 among 5). Why was that not enough?
questions.explain: The program had no error, just unasked questions. Reasoning about what could be true (uneven division, 0 people) found the failures before a customer did.
options: Because one test is always enough if it passes
A test only shows it works for the input tried; reasoning finds the inputs nobody thought to try, like ₦10,000 among 3 or 0 people
Because the test used the wrong numbers

questions.q: Which of these was an unwritten assumption in the first bill splitter?
questions.explain: Nobody said the division would come out even; the code simply treated it as true. With ₦10,000 among 3 it did not, and the shares came out as fractions of a kobo.
options: The output is what each person pays
The total always divides evenly by the number of people

questions.q: What should you do with every assumption you notice?
questions.explain: An assumption that is checked becomes a precondition with a clear refusal. One that is confirmed becomes a documented rule. One that is neither is a bug waiting for the right input.
options: Leave it in your head; it is obvious
Delete the code that depends on it
Either check it in the code or confirm it with a person, and write it down either way
Add a comment saying "should be fine"

questions.q: What is a precondition?
questions.explain: For the bill splitter: people is a whole number, at least 1; the total is a whole number, 0 or more. If they fail, the algorithm should refuse rather than compute.
options: A condition that is true after the algorithm finishes
A condition that must be true before the algorithm runs, or its answer means nothing
The first line of a program
A condition that is never true

questions.q: Which of these is a postcondition of the bill splitter?
questions.explain: A postcondition must be true after the algorithm runs. The other three are preconditions on the input.
options: The number of people is at least 1
The shares add up exactly to the total
The total is a whole number

questions.q: A precondition fails: someone asks to split ₦5,000 among 0 people. What should the program do?
questions.explain: A number that looks like an answer, such as Infinity, NaN or a silent guess, is worse than a clear refusal. It gets saved, shown and used as if it were real.
options: Print Infinity, because that is what the division gives
Treat it as 1 person without saying anything
Refuse with a message that says what is wrong

questions.q: Which of these is an edge case for the bill splitter?
questions.explain: A total smaller than the number of people sits at the edge of what the algorithm handles: someone's share becomes ₦0. The other three are ordinary cases that divide evenly.

questions.q: The rule is "Guests can cancel for free up to 48 hours before check-in." Which is a genuine unknown you should ask about?
questions.explain: "Up to" at the boundary, the check-in time and the time zone all change the answer for real guests. The rule does not say, so guessing would build a decision into the code that nobody made.
options: Whether guests can cancel at all
Whether cancelling exactly 48 hours before is free, and what time of day check-in is
Whether the guest house has rooms

questions.q: What is an invariant?
questions.explain: Because it holds at every step, you can check it after every step. When it breaks, you know exactly which step broke it.
options: A value that is never used
A condition that must hold after every step, not just at the start or the end
An error that cannot be fixed

questions.q: A hall has 500 seats. Which of these is an invariant of the ticket seller?
questions.explain: Selling moves seats from "available" to "sold"; it never creates or destroys them. So the two always add up to the capacity. The other invariant is sold <= 500.

questions.q: The first ticket seller checked sold < capacity before selling and still sold 501 tickets. Why?
questions.explain: With 2 seats left, a group of 3 passed the check. The right precondition for each sale is request <= available.
options: It asked "is there at least one seat?" when the question was "are there enough seats for this whole group?"

questions.q: An invariant check printed "INVARIANT BROKEN" after request 7 and after every request since. Where should you look for the bug?
questions.explain: Once the state is wrong it stays wrong, so every later check fails too. The first failure points at the step that caused it.
options: Request 7, the first one after which it broke
Any request: they are all equally broken

questions.q: What are the three steps of the argument that a loop keeps an invariant, and so is correct?
questions.explain: For "best so far": the first item is the biggest of itself; each new item either replaces biggest or does not, keeping it the biggest seen; when everything is seen, it is the biggest of the list.
options: Write it, run it, ship it
It is true at the start; each step keeps it true; so it is true at the end
It is false at the start; each step makes it true; so it is true at the end
Test the first item, test the last item, test the middle

questions.q: In invariant terms, why is starting "best so far" at 0 wrong for a list of losses like [-2000, -500, -1200]?
questions.explain: An invariant has to be true at the start. 0 is not one of the items, so the argument fails at step 1, and the wrong answer (₦0) follows.
options: The invariant "biggest is the biggest of the items seen" is false from the very start, because 0 is not an item

questions.q: What can an argument about an algorithm do that no number of tests can?
questions.explain: "The shares add up because total = base × people + extra" is true for any total and any number of people. Tests only cover the inputs they try, which is why you use both.
options: Cover every possible input at once

questions.q: A test tries 1,010 combinations of total and people and, for each, checks that the shares add up and differ by at most ₦1. What is this style called?
questions.explain: Instead of writing an expected output for each case, you check rules that must always be true. That lets you test far more inputs than you could ever work out by hand.
options: Property-based testing: checking properties that must hold for every input

questions.q: Two customers try to buy the last concert ticket at the same moment. Both see 1 seat available, and both succeed. What is this called?
questions.explain: Each request is correct on its own; the problem is two of them running at once. Tracing one request never finds it; asking "what if this happens twice, at the same time?" does. Databases solve it with transactions and locks.

questions.q: Why do banks usually store money as a whole number of kobo rather than as naira with decimals?
questions.explain: 0.1 + 0.2 is 0.30000000000000004, not 0.3. Whole numbers of kobo have no such error, so totals always add up.
options: Computers store most decimals approximately, but whole numbers exactly

questions.q: A form asks only for a birth year, and the rule is "18 or older". In 2026, what does reasoning tell you about someone born in 2008?
questions.explain: 2026 - 2008 is 18, but before their birthday they are 17. The obvious code assumes the year difference is the age. Reasoning shows the input itself is not enough.
options: They could be 17 or 18: the input cannot answer the question, so the form should ask for the full date

questions.q: Which set of tests comes from reasoning about the bill splitter, rather than from guessing?
questions.explain: Each precondition, boundary and postcondition you wrote down turns directly into a test. That is how the edge-case table became the test list.
options: One test breaking each precondition, tests on each boundary (remainder 0, 1, 2; total smaller than people; 1 person), and the postcondition checked in every test
A single test with a large number
Whatever inputs the first user tries

questions.q: The splitter gives extra people one extra naira, where extra = total % people. Why are there always enough people to receive them?
questions.explain: Dividing by 3 can leave 0, 1 or 2, never 3 or more. So extra is less than people, and every extra naira has someone to go to.
options: Because a remainder is always smaller than the number you divide by
Because the total is always bigger than the number of people
There are not always enough people

questions.q: ₦2 split among 3 people gives shares of ₦1, ₦1 and ₦0. The postconditions hold. What is the best response?
questions.explain: The edge-case table made you notice it, which is its job. The shares add up and differ by at most ₦1, so the logic is right. How to present a ₦0 share is a decision for the people who own the product.
options: It is a bug: change the algorithm so nobody pays ₦0
The algorithm is consistent; whether a ₦0 share should be shown is a product question to ask the owner

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Division gives a decimal, and the computer stores it approximately, hence the 5 at the end. Nobody can pay that, which is why the splitter rounds down and hands out the remainder.

questions.q: A precondition is broken. What does this print?
questions.explain: JavaScript does not stop on division by zero: it gives Infinity, and 0 ÷ 0 gives NaN. Both look like values and flow on into the program, which is why the precondition must be checked first.
options:
Error: division by zero
Error: division by zero

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Math.floor rounds 2,333.33… down to 2,333. The remainder of 7,000 ÷ 3 is 1, because 2,333 × 3 = 6,999.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: 10,001 ÷ 3 is 3,333 with remainder 2, so the first two people pay ₦1 more. 3,334 + 3,334 + 3,333 = 10,001.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: base is 0 and extra is 2, so the first two people pay ₦1 and the third ₦0. The shares still add up to 2. (The trailing space comes from adding " " after each share.)

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The precondition is checked first, so the division never happens. A clear refusal instead of Infinity.
options: Refused: the total cannot be negative

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Any number divided by 1 leaves its fractional part as the remainder. So x % 1 !== 0 is a way to ask "is x not a whole number?".

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: After the first request, 99 are sold, and 99 < 100 lets the group of 4 through, making 103. The check asked "is there one seat?", not "are there four?".

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The first group of 2 fits (97 + 2 = 99 sold, 1 left). The second group of 2 does not, so it is refused. The single ticket fits the last seat: 100 sold, 0 left. sold + available is 100 after every step.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The invariant holds on every line: best is the biggest of the profits seen so far. -300 is bigger than -800, and -1500 is not bigger than -300.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: 0.1 cannot be stored exactly, so multiplying it carries the error. Whole numbers are exact. That is why money is best kept in whole kobo.

questions.q: The number of people came from a form as text. What does this print?
questions.explain: Division converts the text to a number, so the first line happens to work. + glues text, so "4" + 1 is "41". An unchecked assumption that works in one place breaks silently in another.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: 6 − 4 = 2, then 2 − 3 = −1: the invariant "stock is never negative" breaks on the sale of 3. The delivery brings it back to 4, which hides the problem if you only look at the end.

questions.q: Add the precondition "at least 1 person" before the division. With the inputs given, the program must print Refused: need at least 1 person instead of Infinity.
questions.explain: Check the precondition first and refuse clearly. The division only runs when its answer can mean something.

questions.q: Split ₦7,000 among 3 people in whole naira, the first people paying ₦1 more if it does not divide evenly. Print one line per person: Person 1 pays ₦2334, Person 2 pays ₦2333, Person 3 pays ₦2333.
questions.explain: 7,000 ÷ 3 is 2,333 with remainder 1, so one person pays ₦2,334. The shares add up to 7,000 exactly.
questions.expected:
Person 1 pays ₦2334
Person 2 pays ₦2333
Person 3 pays ₦2333

questions.q: The splitter works, but nothing checks its postcondition. Keep a running sum of the shares and, after the loop, print Adds up: true by comparing the sum with the total.
questions.explain: A postcondition you print is one you can see holding. sum === total gives true or false, so the program reports its own verdict.

questions.q: This seller only checks that at least one seat is left, so it oversells. Change the condition so a request is only sold when there are enough seats for all of it. The output must be Sold 2, Refused 3, Sold 1 and then Sold: 100.
questions.explain: The right precondition for a sale is request <= available. With it, the invariant sold <= capacity can never break.

questions.q: Add an invariant check inside the loop: after each change, if the stock is below 0, print Negative stock after followed by the change. With the events given, the output must be Negative stock after -5 and then Final: 3.
questions.explain: The final stock of 3 looks fine. Only a check after every step shows that the sale of 5 happened when there were only 2 bags.

questions.q: Add the precondition "the total must be whole naira". For the input given, the program must print Refused: use whole numbers.
questions.explain: total % 1 is the part after the decimal point. If it is not 0, the total is not a whole number, and the precondition fails.

questions.q: Check the splitter's "adds up" property on many inputs: every total from 0 to 20 with every group size from 1 to 5. Count the cases checked and the ones that fail, and print Checked 105 cases, 0 failed.
questions.explain: 21 totals times 5 group sizes is 105 cases. Checking a property on every one of them backs up the argument that the shares always add up.

questions.q: Only the birth year is known, and the rule is "18 or older". In 2026, a difference of 19 or more is safe to allow, 18 cannot be decided, and less is refused. For a birth year of 2008 it must print ask for the full date of birth.
questions.explain: With the year alone, someone with a difference of 18 may not have had their birthday yet. The honest answer is "cannot tell", and the real fix is to collect the full date.
questions.expected: ask for the full date of birth
